item.title: kw-bench shows frontier models solve complex VAT reconstruction in minutes
item.description:
kw-bench shows frontier models solve complex VAT reconstruction in minutes

A new benchmark, kw-bench, evaluates coding‑agent harnesses on real‑world investigative knowledge work.

🔍 Overview

  • Each new generation of frontier model pushes the edge of what is possible.
  • A growing body of work treats the coding‑agent harness as infrastructure for knowledge work rather than a coding tool, and a new wave of benchmarks tests it there.
  • kw-bench is built from real engagements specialists described to us and focuses on the expensive, investigative part of knowledge work.

🧩 Benchmark Design

  • First task family: a five‑year VAT reconstruction across three generations of SAP – legacy ECC, a partial S/4HANA migration and a consultant’s redesign.
  • Input: raw system extracts (page headers, local number formats, partial link tables) with no documentation of how anything connects.
  • Grading is deterministic, with no LLM judge.

⚙️ Results

Harness Model Score Time (minutes)
Claude Code DeepSeek v4.1 Flash 0.00 120 (2 hours)
Codex DeepSeek v4.1 Flash 0.00 120 (2 hours)
OpenCode DeepSeek v4.1 Flash 0.542 120 (2 hours)
micro‑cc DeepSeek v4.1 Flash 0.528 120 (2 hours)
micro‑cc Claude Opus 5.5 0.9986 22
Claude Code Claude Opus 5.5 1.000 25
  • What defeated the two lab harnesses on DeepSeek was inertia: keeping many weak signals alive across a long session.
  • On a frontier model the task collapses, delivering near‑perfect scores in a fraction of the time.

🚀 Implications

  • A weeks‑long engagement now costs minutes and a few dollars.
  • Below the frontier, the harness decides how far a model gets; with a matching harness, frontier models achieve essentially perfect performance.
  • This highlights the importance of both model capability and harness design for investigative knowledge‑work automation.

📊 Scoring Method

  • Scores are deterministic; there is no LLM judge involved.
  • The benchmark treats the answer as hidden in incomplete and inconsistent evidence that must be recovered and defended to the cent.

#AIbenchmark #knowledgework #frontiermodels #codingagents

Source: kw-bench: Breaking Frontier Harnesses on Real-World Tasks Source: Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?

item.title: New Handoff State Continuity Benchmark Evaluates AI Agent Task Takeover
item.description:
New Handoff State Continuity Benchmark Evaluates AI Agent Task Takeover

A benchmark called the Handoff State Continuity Benchmark (HSC‑Bench) was introduced to measure how well AI agents can take over tasks from one another.

🔍 Overview

  • Agents often need to pass responsibility before a long‑running task is finished.
  • The receiving model must build on prior decisions, observations, and actions while satisfying the remaining requirements.
  • Traditional task‑success and memory‑retention scores do not capture the quality of this transition.

🧩 Benchmark Design

  • HSC‑Bench contains 1,039 tasks.
  • It evaluates two complementary aspects of task takeover:
    • Recovering relevant repository evidence.
    • Continuing from established conversational, tool, and file‑work state.

⚙️ Findings

  • Six receiving models were compared.
  • Structured handoff state improved repository evidence recovery for every model.
  • It also improved continuation performance for most models.
  • The strongest receivers differed between the two evaluation tracks, indicating that evidence‑recovery rankings alone do not characterize performance when continuing from inherited state.
  • By checking subsequent responses and actions, HSC‑Bench assesses both access to prior evidence and adherence to earlier commitments and completed work.

💡 Implications

  • HSC‑Bench provides a basis for selecting receiving models based on the specific handoff requirements of a project.
  • It also supports assessing handoff representations to ensure that the work to be carried forward is preserved accurately.

#AIagents #Benchmark #HSCBench

Source: Benchmarking Task Takeover Across Agent Handoffs

item.title: Audit Reveals Specification-Oracle Gap in Coding-Agent Benchmarks
item.description:
Audit Reveals Specification-Oracle Gap in Coding-Agent Benchmarks

Coding‑agent benchmarks often phrase a task in natural language while grading it with upstream tests that may require hidden implementation details.

🔍 Overview

  • Benchmarks describe the request in plain text but validate output using tests taken from the original project.
  • Passing those tests can need information the description never provides, such as a constant’s name, a module path, or an exact error message.

🧩 Specification‑Oracle Gap

  • This mismatch is called a specification‑oracle gap.
  • Where the gap exists, a benchmark unintentionally measures an agent’s ability to reproduce upstream implementation details rather than just solving the described problem.

⚙️ How the Gap Was Audited

  • The authors formalised the gap and the inconsistencies introduced by chains of dependent tasks.
  • They built a static audit covering five programming languages that classifies every name‑, path‑, and literal‑level dependency of every scored test.
  • The audit achieved held‑out precision of 89.2 % and recall of 92.9 %.

📊 Findings

  • SWE‑Milestone (98 graded milestones, 35 published runs):
    • 25 milestones contain a test depending on an unstated, non‑inferable name or path.
    • Build units with such a hidden dependency fail in 80.6 % of runs, versus 48.4 % for comparable units without one.
    • Removing a single hidden name from the reference prevents compilation in 126 of 128 cases.
  • The leaderboard ranking remains robust after removing the affected tests, but scores shift within repositories and tend to favour agents that replicate upstream names.
  • Across four additional benchmarks:
    • A third or more of tasks are affected when specifications come from release notes or LLM summaries.
    • Almost none are affected when tasks are screened or written expressly for their tests.
    • The cost of the gap varies with how the harness grades the solutions.

🚀 Release

  • The authors have released the static audit, corrected filter lists, and specification addenda for the community to use.

#AIagents #Benchmarking #SoftwareEngineering #Evaluation

Source: What the Specification Did Not Say: Specification-Oracle Gaps in Test-Graded Coding-Agent Benchmarks

item.title: Preregistered Evaluation of Language Models on Numeric Values in Norwegian Law
item.description:
Preregistered Evaluation of Language Models on Numeric Values in Norwegian Law

A preregistered study evaluated language models on extracting numeric values from Norwegian statutes, regulations, and parliamentary decisions.

🔍 Overview

  • 916 items were extracted mechanically from Lovdata’s open data, each carrying the dated history of its provision.
  • The task asked language models for numeric values (NOK amounts, percentages, multiples of the National Insurance basic amount (G), and age limits) at a stated date.
  • Each answer can be classified as correct, outdated, wrong, or uninterpretable.

⚙️ Study Design

  • Two preregistered runs were performed on the same items.
  • First run: involved five models (names listed publicly only after local analysis). Hypothesis H1 (outdated answers more frequent for values after a model’s cutoff) could not be tested in substance; H2 and H3 were inconclusive.
  • Second run: preregistered and published before any calls, analysing eight models.

📊 Results

  • The pooled primary test of H1 in the second run supported the hypothesis (d = 17.8 percentage points, 95 % CI [7.7, 28.9], p = 0.0001).
  • In preregistered sensitivity analysis S8 (outdated counted only for the most recent differing value), d = 3.9 [-3.6, 12.7] (p = 0.1754), an interval that contains 0, so support for H1 is not robust.
  • H1 was supported in every other preregistered sensitivity analysis, but S8 is the only one giving both groups a single target value.
  • Share of outdated answers equal to the most recent value (H2) was 56.1 % [46.6, 65.0], an interval that contains 0.5.
  • The pooled test of a lower share correct in Nynorsk than in Bokmål (H3) was inconclusive.

Model Performance (Correct on Primary Items)

Model Correct %
Opus 5.5 46.7 %
Sonnet 4.6 40.2 %
  • Several models, among them Haiku 4.5, gave mostly uninterpretable answers.

📁 Data Availability

  • Items and keys are withheld.
  • Item IDs, per‑answer classes, code, and results are available on Zenodo.

#AIEvaluation #LanguageModels #NorwegianLaw #Preregistration

Source: norregel: a preregistered benchmark of dated numeric values in Norwegian law

item.title: Guideline-Enhanced GPT‑4.1 Agent Hits 67.5% Pass⁴ on τ²‑bench Retail
item.description:
Guideline-Enhanced GPT‑4.1 Agent Hits 67.5% Pass⁴ on τ²‑bench Retail

A basic retail customer‑service agent built on GPT‑4.1, augmented with automatically extracted behavioral guidelines via the ALTK‑Evolve system, achieved a 67.5 % Pass⁴ score on the τ²‑bench benchmark, outperforming every other retail entry in the October 12 2026 leaderboard snapshot.

🔍 Overview

  • τ²‑bench (from Sierra) evaluates how well an LLM‑based agent handles customer‑service conversations under realistic constraints.
  • Each task pairs the agent with an LLM‑simulated customer, a set of domain tools (order lookup, refund issuance, flight rebooking), and a written policy document the agent must follow.
  • The benchmark includes two domains: Retail (40 test tasks) and Airline (20 test tasks).
  • In the experiment the agent runs on the benchmark’s stock ReAct scaffold (a THINK → ACT loop) using gpt‑4.1 as the agent model and gpt‑5.5 as the customer‑simulator.

🧩 How it works

  • ALTK‑Evolve builds a playbook of short behavioral rules (e.g., how to authenticate a customer, confirm a transaction, handle a return) by:
    1. Running the baseline ReAct agent on the τ²‑bench training tasks.
    2. Analyzing the agent’s training‑task attempts with the same gpt‑4.1 model.
    3. Distilling successes and failures into concise guidelines, each tagged with a support count (the number of distinct training tasks it appeared in).
  • The extracted guidelines are appended to the system prompt of the agent for subsequent conversations; no weight updates or human annotation are required.
  • Three guideline‑selection configurations are evaluated:
    • baseline – no guidelines.
    • sup3 – keep only guidelines with support ≥ 3 (high‑confidence core).
    • lossless – keep every guideline (support ≥ 1).

📈 Results

Domain Configuration Mean Accuracy Pass⁴ # Guidelines
Retail (40) baseline 78.1 % 57.5 % 0
Retail (40) sup3 (support ≥ 3) 78.8 % (+0.7) 60.0 % (+2.5) 31
Retail (40) lossless (all) 82.5 % (+4.4) 67.5 % (+10.0) 292
Airline (20) baseline 57.5 % 35.0 % 0
Airline (20) sup3 (support ≥ 3) 60.0 % (+2.5) 45.0 % (+10.0) 14
Airline (20) lossless (all) 65.0 % (+7.5) 40.0 % (+5.0) 101
  • The lossless configuration improves Retail Pass⁴ by 10 percentage points, reaching the top of the October 12 2026 leaderboard.
  • All improvements come without any model fine‑tuning; the same gpt‑4.1 model powers both guideline extraction and the agent itself.

💡 Why it matters

  • Demonstrates that automatic rule extraction from agent trajectories can substantially raise performance on realistic customer‑service benchmarks.
  • Shows a path to stronger agents without expensive weight updates or human‑in‑the‑loop annotation.
  • Highlights the utility of the ReAct scaffold combined with a concise, data‑driven prompt playbook.

#GPT4 #CustomerServiceAI #Benchmark #PromptEngineering

Source: ALTK-Evolve: How learned memory tops the τ²-bench leaderboard on customer service tasks without a frontier model

item.title: Underdog Saluki 27B 1.0 Quantized Model Beats Original on Tool-Calling Test
item.description:
Underdog Saluki 27B 1.0 Quantized Model Beats Original on Tool-Calling Test

A new 2‑bit quantized version of the Qwen3.8‑27B model, Underdog Saluki 27B 1.0, has been released. At 7.89 GB it outperforms the 54 GB original on a 120‑task tool‑calling benchmark, though its math capabilities are considerably weaker.

🔍 Overview

  • Model name: Underdog Saluki 27B 1.0
  • Base model: Qwen3.8‑27B
  • Quantization format: 2‑bit GGUF
  • File size: 7.89 GB

🧩 How it works

  • Uses a 2‑bit GGUF representation to compress the 27 billion‑parameter model.
  • No changes to the underlying architecture; only the weight representation is reduced.

⚙️ Key details

  • Size reduction: from the original 54 GB to 7.89 GB (≈ 85 % smaller).
  • Task suite: evaluated on a 120‑task tool‑calling benchmark.
  • Math performance: reported as “loses badly on math” compared with the original.

📊 Performance

  • Tool‑calling: beats the 54 GB original on the 120‑task test.
  • Mathematical reasoning: underperforms the original model significantly.

💡 Why it matters

  • Shows that aggressive quantization can retain or improve performance on specific downstream tasks (tool‑calling) while sacrificing others (math).
  • Provides a lightweight alternative for developers needing a smaller model footprint for tool‑calling applications.
  • Highlights the importance of task‑specific evaluation when deploying highly compressed models.

#Quantization #LargeLanguageModels #ToolCalling #ModelCompression

Source: AI News: Saturday, October 10, 2026

item.title: ThinkingBox Benchmark Reveals Gaps Between LLM Agent Tool Calls and Database State
item.description:
ThinkingBox Benchmark Reveals Gaps Between LLM Agent Tool Calls and Database State

A joint Microsoft‑Hugging Face blog introduces ThinkingBox, a benchmark that runs LLM agents against isolated tool sessions, then grades the resulting backend database state and side effects.

🔍 Overview

  • The blog is co‑authored by Microsoft and Hugging Face, with thanks to Tommy Guy, Sergio Paniego, and former interns Zhuochun Li, Ali Keramati, and Youngmin Ko.
  • Figure 1 shows the workflow: an agent interacts with MCP tool sessions, and a grader checks the terminal backend state and side effects.

🧩 How it works

  • Each of the 507 stateful business workflows is executed 20 times from an identical clean backend.
  • Agents invoke tools (e.g., order lookup, tracking, policy search) and produce final responses.
  • An AI grader examines the terminal database state rather than just the sequence of tool calls.
  • Example: a retail‑support task where an agent makes nine well‑formed tool calls but leaves the ticket status as solved while the required end state is hold.
  • The executable check fails because the database disagrees with the claimed outcome.

⚙️ Key details

  • Trials: 121 680 valid trials across 12 LLM models.
  • Failures: 79 853 attempts failed the executable checks.
  • Among failures:
    • 67.24 % terminated cleanly, invoked a state‑changing tool, and reported no final tool error.
    • 77.61 % had wrong field values.
    • 43.30 % produced unintended extra effects.
    • 25.36 % missed required effects.
  • Performance snapshot (overall pass % where the backend state matched the claim):
Model Overall Pass % Retail Pass % Auto‑Insurance Pass %
Claude Opus 5.5 67.16 — —
Claude Opus 5 (two‑thirds of a point below 5.5) — —
Claude Opus 4.6 — 68.62 8.30
Kimi‑K3 (open‑weights) — (within a point of GPT‑6‑Astra) —
  • Observed 20/20: the literal count of how many of the 507 tasks passed all 20 runs is reported.

💡 Why it matters

  • Final responses and valid tool calls are only proxies; the database state is the evidence.
  • A trajectory is a claim, and repetition is the trust test – an agent that succeeds once but fails later is not a reliable refund agent.
  • The benchmark highlights that many agents appear correct by tool‑call metrics yet leave incorrect values, unintended side effects, or missing required changes in the backend.
  • Domain matters: the same model can score dramatically different percentages on retail versus auto‑insurance tasks.

All statements are drawn directly from the provided evidence.

#ThinkingBox #LLM #AIAgents #Benchmark

Source: The Agent Said It Was Done. The Database Disagreed.
